title: Kranti Gaud Fined 10% of Match Fee for Send-Off in Women's Asia Cup Final
excerpt: The India pacer was docked part of her match fee and handed one demerit point for gesturing opener Imesha Dulani toward the pavilion during Sunday's final against Sri Lanka in Dubai.
body:
• India pacer Kranti Gaud has been fined 10% of her match fee for a Level 1 breach of the ICC Code of Conduct during the Women's T20 Asia Cup final against Sri Lanka in Dubai.
  • The offence: after dismissing opener Imesha Dulani in the first over of Sri Lanka's chase, Gaud gestured toward the pavilion — a send-off that fell foul of Article 2.5.
  • One demerit point has been added to Gaud's disciplinary record — her first offence in a 24-month period. She admitted the charge and accepted the sanction, so no formal hearing was needed.
  • India beat Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final to claim a record-extending eighth Women's Asia Cup title; Pakistan were separately fined 5% of their match fee for a slow over-rate in the semi-final.

India fast bowler Kranti Gaud has been fined 10% of her match fee and handed one demerit point for giving a send-off to Sri Lanka opener Imesha Dulani during the Women's T20 Asia Cup final in Dubai, the International Cricket Council confirmed on Monday.

The incident came in the first over of Sri Lanka's innings on Sunday, when Gaud castled Dulani and then gestured in the direction of the pavilion. She was found guilty of breaching Level 1 of Article 2.5 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to "using language, actions or gestures which disparage, or which could provoke an aggressive reaction from a batter upon his/her dismissal during an international match".

Gaud admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by match referee Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees, so there was no need for a formal hearing, according to ESPNcricinfo and an ANI report. The charges were levelled by on-field umpires Saleema Imtiaz and Shathira Jakir Jesy, third umpire Rokeya Sultana and fourth umpire Humaira Farah. It was Gaud's first offence in a 24-month period.

"India pacer Kranti Gaud has been fined 10 per cent of her match fee for breaching Level 1 of the ICC Code of Conduct during the Women's Asia Cup final against Sri Lanka in Dubai on Sunday."

— International Cricket Council statement, via ANI

Context & Background

The disciplinary call arrived barely a day after India sealed the title at the Dubai International Stadium, defeating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final to secure a record-extending eighth Women's Asia Cup crown — reclaiming the trophy after Sri Lanka had beaten them in the 2024 final. Gaud played her part in the victory, bowling a couple of overs for eight runs and claiming the wicket that triggered the controversy.

Level 1 breaches carry a minimum penalty of an official reprimand, a maximum of 50% of a player's match fee, and one or two demerit points — Gaud's 10% fine and single demerit point fall at the lighter end of that range, reflecting a first offence and a prompt admission.

The final also carried off-field drama of its own: India declined to accept the trophy from Asian Cricket Council President Mohsin Naqvi, who also serves as Pakistan's interior minister, according to an IANS report.

Impact & Analysis

For Gaud, the sanction is a blemish on what has been a strong tournament — a small financial penalty and a single demerit point that sits on her disciplinary record for two years. Because she accepted the proposed sanction, the matter is closed with no formal hearing and no risk of escalation.

More broadly, the ruling is another reminder of the ICC's tightening posture on send-offs and aggressive gestures after dismissals in the women's game. With millions of viewers watching a final, a gesture toward the pavilion is treated as disparaging conduct whether or not the batter reacts, and the all-women umpiring panel in Dubai was not inclined to let it slide.

Diaspora Angle

The final was played in front of a large South Asian expatriate crowd in Dubai, where India–Sri Lanka contests routinely feel like home games for both sides. For the Indian diaspora across the Gulf, North America and Europe, the result was double-edged — an eighth title to celebrate, and a reminder that women's cricket now draws the same scrutiny, and the same passionate debate, as the men's game. The Dulani dismissal has already become one of the most discussed moments of the final on diaspora cricket forums and social feeds.

What's Next

The demerit point stays on Gaud's record for a rolling 24-month period, and any repeat offence would bring a heavier sanction under the ICC's escalating scale. India, meanwhile, leave Dubai as Asia Cup champions again — with momentum restored after the 2024 defeat and the title defence already being eyed. The team will hope its next headlines come from the scoreboard rather than the match referee's report.

nri_angle: India's 72-run final win over Sri Lanka thrilled South Asian diaspora fans, and the Dubai final — played before a large expatriate crowd — put women's cricket's rising diaspora audience and the tightening policing of send-offs squarely in the spotlight.
